Authentication and sessions

Source: vignettes/authorization.Rmd
authorization.Rmd

Keep each person’s database connections and query results in their Shiny session. Reactive outputs follow sign-in changes; if you cache data, clear it when users sign out or change account.

For a complete app with sign-in setup, choose your source in Getting started.

Follow sign-in changes

Create connection helpers inside server() and call con() in each render or reactive expression that queries the database. The helper reuses the connection. When the authorization or Shiny session ends, it stops returning the connection and calls the driver’s cleanup method.

Cleanup depends on the driver. In particular, a retained brickster connection can still submit requests with its copied token after sign-out. Call con() before each operation; see the Databricks guide.

Put API client calls inside reactive expressions too. This lets Shiny update the output when the selected account changes.

Save query results

If you keep results in reactiveVal(), eventReactive(), or another cache, clear or hide them when the user signs out or changes account. Closing a database connection doesn’t erase data the app has already fetched. A cache keyed only by SQL text can share protected results between users.

The source checkout’s playground/example-query-button.R shows a query button that clears results on sign-out, account changes, and loss of required permissions.

Request permissions

OAuth scopes describe the permissions your app requests during sign-in. Set them on the shinyOAuth client. The presets supply defaults for the selected services.

A helper’s required_scopes checks for permissions before use. It doesn’t request additional consent or add database privileges. The shinyOAuth client still enforces its configured requirements.

Microsoft’s /.default requests the registration’s configured permissions. It isn’t a granted permission name, so don’t put it in required_scopes. The Snowflake guide describes its role scopes.

Use an existing login

You can keep an existing shinyOAuth provider, client, UI, and server module. The *_client() helpers are optional presets.

The token must be intended for the database or API you’re calling. Named token targets let one authorization obtain tokens for different services, each with its own permission requirements. Microsoft’s presets use names such as "sql" and "storage".

For an existing SQL target named "reporting", select it explicitly:

con <- oauth_db_azure_sql(
  auth$connection,
  server = "example.database.windows.net",
  database = "Reporting",
  target = "reporting"
)

For a client without named targets, use target = NULL with a suitable default token. The Fabric guide shows how to map services to your client’s targets.

Select among several accounts

Use shinyOAuth’s connection manager when a user needs to keep several authorizations and choose between them. vignette("multiple-authorizations", package = "shinyOAuth") covers the manager setup.

Pass a function that selects the database authorization:

con <- oauth_db_azure_sql(
  function() auth$connection(shiny::req(input$authorization_id)),
  server = "example.database.windows.net",
  database = "Reporting"
)

Use the connection_id values from auth$connections() in the account selector. These identify saved authorizations, rather than token targets such as "sql".

You can create separate helpers for different selected accounts. The source checkout’s playground/example-two-authorizations.R shows independent SQL and Databricks authorizations.

Inspect HTTP errors

BigQuery, PostgREST and ClickHouse HTTP failures raise shinyOAuthDB_request_failed. Catch that condition inside the Shiny operation to inspect its status. When the response supplies a recognized service code or a UUID request identifier, the condition also includes service_code and request_id; unavailable or rejected values are NULL.

For example, BigQuery can report invalidQuery or accessDenied, PostgREST can report SQLSTATE 42P01, and ClickHouse can report a numeric exception code. The condition excludes server messages, response bodies and credentials.

Token refresh and background work

shinyOAuth renews tokens. Call con() before each operation so the helper can check the current authorization and replace a connection when needed. Each source guide describes how its client uses refreshed credentials.

If refresh is already running, ordinary reactive outputs wait and can resume when it finishes. A button-triggered query may need another click. min_valid_for asks for enough token lifetime at the start of an operation; it doesn’t guarantee validity for a whole query.

Keep live connections and token callbacks in the Shiny session that created them. For background work, use the database package’s supported approach and check the current authorization before displaying a result. Local sign-out doesn’t necessarily invalidate a copied token or cancel work already submitted to a platform.
